extracted.intended_audience: General literate public (18th-century readers), merchants, householders, and family correspondents
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of personal letters and essays giving moral, legal, commercial, and household advice. Includes norms for punishment and law, conduct in war and privateering, merchant honesty, and domestic economy and virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishments should be proportioned to offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly argues against excessive punishments (example: hanging for stealing gauze worth fourteen shillings and threepence) and holds that punishment beyond the merit of the offence is 'so much punishment of innocence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer avoiding wrongful punishment of the innocent
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better that many guilty persons escape than that one innocent person should suffer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The maxim—'better a hundred guilty persons should escape than that one innocent person should suffer'—is presented as a long-approved principle that should constrain penal policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law must not commit unjust acts in punishing crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Society should not punish a social delict by committing a crime against nature (i.e., an unjust or monstrous punishment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted as a rhetorical question: 'Doit-on punir un délit contre la société par un crime contre la nature?'—laws that abuse power and commence tyranny by inflicting cruel punishments are condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of punishments to ensure execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive severity of laws prevents their execution and often forces a preference for impunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Montesquieu: 'L'atrocité des loix en empêche l'exécution... When the punishment is excessive, it is frequently necessary to prefer impunity.' Thus moderation can increase enforceability and reduce crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment beyond merit is punishment of innocence
rubrics_metrics.description: Any punishment inflicted beyond the merit of the offence constitutes punishment of innocence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author uses the example of disproportionate capital punishment for petty thefts to underline that excessive penalties effectively punish innocent excess and should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public injustice and state policy influence private crime
rubrics_metrics.description: A government's oppressive or unjust conduct (domestic oppression, unjust wars, monopolies) contributes to depravity and crime among the populace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay points to monopolizing treatment of Ireland, merchant plundering in the Indies, and wars of rapine as causes that encourage theft and corruption among citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: States and nations are morally accountable like individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation that wages unjust war or commissions privateers is comparable to a gang of robbers and should be judged by the same moral standard as individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author insists justice is due between nations as between citizens: unjust national behavior (privateering, confiscations) undermines domestic morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merchants should assess the justice of wars before commissioning privateers
rubrics_metrics.description: Merchants ought to consider well the justice of a war before hiring or commissioning vessels to prey on fellow merchants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text reproaches merchants who fit out privateers to attack neighbours for profit, urging them to examine whether it is right to employ 'a gang of ruffians' to plunder others.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-sanctioned privateering corrupts society
rubrics_metrics.description: Commissioning private armed vessels (privateers) to take prizes encourages a national appetite for plunder that extends domestically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: seven hundred privateers were commissioned in a war; the author links privateering to increased inclination to steal at home and moral corrosion.

rubrics_metrics.name: International humane rules in war (protect noncombatants and commerce)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treaties should protect unarmed merchant ships and noncombatant civilians, allowing merchants and certain civilians to continue their employments unmolested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited treaty article offered by the United States and accepted by the king of Prussia: unarmed merchant vessels and civilians such as artisans and farmers should not be molested; privateers should not be commissioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soldiers and officers should not accept moral abdication
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that a military man must not inquire whether a war is just is dangerous; soldiers and officers have moral responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes the maxim that soldiers merely execute orders, arguing it enables tyrants and that conscientious officers may resign rather than participate in unjust actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscripted servicemen suffer loss of moral agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Private soldiers and sailors conscripted or compelled into service are ‘slaves for life’ and may be unable to judge for themselves about the justice of orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text laments the fate of forcibly impressed sailors and soldiers forced to commit possibly unjust acts, contrasting their condition with free merchants who can choose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventive punishment cannot justify disproportionate penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Using extreme punishment merely to deter others (prevent crimes) is not a valid excuse for disproportionate sentencing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Judge Burnet's reply to a horse-stealer—'thou art not to be hanged only for stealing a horse, but that horses may not be stolen'—which the author treats as brutal and unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restitution and refusal to profit from wartime plunder are virtuous
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusing to profit from prize goods and seeking to make restitution to those wronged is morally commendable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of a Quaker part-owner who advertises to find those who lost property to make restitution—praised as conscientious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value usefulness and domestic virtue over ornament and fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the character and usefulness of a good housewife (industry, skill) to the superficial advantages of being a fashionable gentlewoman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin's choice of a spinning-wheel over a teatable as a gift exemplifies valuing practical domestic skills above mere appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty is a prime female virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Modesty enhances a woman's character; its absence renders beauty disagreeable and odious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author writes that modesty can make even homeliness amiable and that the want of modesty 'infallibly renders the most perfect beauty disagreeable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry, frugality, and prudent economy in a spouse are an economic asset
rubrics_metrics.description: A wife's industry, frugality, and prudent economy function, for a tradesman, as a 'fortune'—crucial to household prosperity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to family: if a wife performs her household duties steadily and economically, the household will flourish even without a monetary dowry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose gifts and household purchases to promote useful economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Select household items and gifts that are useful and promote industry (e.g., spinning-wheel) rather than costly ornaments that lead to debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative of runaway consumerism: small purchases (glass, chairs, maid, clock, pacing mare) cumulatively ruin finances; replacing them with practical items restores solvency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid status-driven consumerism; practice frugality to regain solvency
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandoning vanity purchases (maids, fashionable furniture, a pacing mare) and selling unnecessary luxuries is the route to financial recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The letter from Anthony Afterwit chronicles deliberate economizing—turning away the maid, selling the mare, buying a milch-cow, repurposing items—to pay debts and recover stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resourcefulness and repurposing in household management
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical ingenuity—repurposing items (e.g., transforming a clock into an hourglass) and adapting existing furniture—serves household economy and appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer describes intentionally converting and reusing items to maintain respectable appearance while economizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and accommodate the elderly in housing and possessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Old people should be allowed their own way and remain in their homes; their few fine things should not be forced to be sold as they provide comfort and may secure future care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: do not remove old people from their houses; preserve their possessions because expectation of inheritance may encourage relatives to be tender and helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and quality in manufacture and trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers should never slight manufacture or attempt to deceive by appearance; produce good goods before sending to market and avoid counterfeiting marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to a soap-maker: make the soap faithfully so he can confidently put his mark on it; do not use the Franklin arms (counterfeiting) and avoid selling inferior goods that harm reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good works are duties of gratitude, not means to merit heaven
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform acts of service to others as repayment of received kindnesses and as duty to fellow humans, not as a way to earn salvation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a letter to Whitefield, the author states he sees good works as paying debts and expressions of gratitude to God and mankind, not as a transactional means of meriting heaven.
